name: Chasteberry (Vitex agnus-castus fruit extract)
short: Case report: disordered hormones and signs of mild ovarian hyperstimulation when taken during IVF. Review: avoid in pregnancy or breastfeeding; may interfere with dopamine blockers (theory).
text: Fertility treatment and hormones (case report): a 1994 report describes a woman having unstimulated in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) cycles who took Vitex agnus castus at the start of her fourth cycle; in that cycle her blood gonadotrophin and ovarian hormone measurements were disordered, three eggs were collected and one embryo resulted but no pregnancy followed, and she had symptoms suggestive of mild ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome. Her next two cycles were normal, and the authors say they do not advocate this herbal medicine to promote normal ovarian function. Interactions and pregnancy: a 2005 systematic review of all available human safety data on single-herb preparations (clinical trials, postmarketing surveillance, surveys and spontaneous reporting schemes) found that no drug interactions had been reported, but states that in theory chasteberry might interfere with dopaminergic antagonists (dopamine-blocking medicines) and that its use should be avoided during pregnancy or lactation. A 2008 systematic review on pregnancy and lactation found only poor evidence, from theory, expert opinion and laboratory studies, that chasteberry may have oestrogen-like and progesterone-like activity and uterine stimulant activity, and found that expert opinion conflicts on whether it increases or decreases breast-milk production. A 2005 review of chasteberry likewise says no herb-drug interactions have been reported but advises caution when it is used with dopamine agonists or antagonists, and lists minor reported adverse effects including gastrointestinal complaints, dizziness and dry mouth; a 2003 review reports that an extract lowered serum prolactin in a double-blind placebo-controlled study and attributes this to dopamine-like compounds in the fruit. None of the cited abstracts reports a study of chasteberry taken with hormonal contraceptives, hormone therapy or fertility drugs. Adverse events: the 2005 review found adverse events mild and reversible, most often nausea, headache, gastrointestinal disturbances, menstrual disorders, acne, itching and red skin rash, and a 2013 systematic review of 12 randomised trials described them as mild and generally infrequent. In a placebo-controlled trial in 170 women with premenstrual syndrome, 7 reported mild adverse events (4 on chasteberry, 3 on placebo), none of which led to stopping treatment; no serious adverse event occurred in either group of a 217-woman trial in China; and in a trial against vitamin B6 (90 women on chasteberry, 85 on vitamin B6), adverse events (gastrointestinal and lower abdominal complaints, skin reactions and short-lived headache) occurred in 12 women on chasteberry and 5 on vitamin B6, and no serious adverse events were observed.
